messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rodrigo is a 62-year-old married surgeon of Colombian descent who has practiced cardiothoracic surgery at a large metropolitan hospital for over thirty years. He came to the clinic six weeks after a severe motor vehicle accident that occurred on a rain-slicked interstate during his evening commute. A commercial truck drifted from its lane and struck Rodrigo's sedan at highway speed, spinning the vehicle across two lanes before it came to rest against a concrete median barrier. He was conscious throughout, pinned briefly behind the collapsed steering column, aware of the hiss of the engine and the smell of something burning. The colleague who had been riding with him, a fellow surgeon named Marcus, was seriously injured and airlifted from the scene. It was the sight of Marcus, motionless and bleeding against the crumpled passenger door, that Rodrigo cannot stop seeing.

In the days immediately following the accident, Rodrigo noticed that the memories did not behave the way memories should. Rather than fading with distance, they arrived with a sharpness that outstripped anything else in his experience — more vivid, he said, than the birth of his children, more present than any moment he could voluntarily summon. The memory forces its way into his mind without invitation, arriving whole and sudden: the sound of impact, Marcus's face, the texture of the deflated airbag fabric against his palm as he tried to push himself free. That specific tactile quality — a coarse, powdery synthetic weave — has become a reliable portal back into the event. When he encounters anything with a similar texture at work, the rough edge of a surgical drape or the non-slip grip of a instrument tray, the memory surges forward without warning, and he finds himself back on that highway rather than in the operating theatre. Even seeing Marcus, who survived and has returned to limited duties, can be enough. A glimpse of him in the corridor or the sound of his voice from another room restores the scene with a completeness that Rodrigo finds almost unbearable. Similarly, the sight of badly damaged vehicles — passed on the highway, glimpsed on the evening news — carries the same force, the imagery of crumpled metal now inseparable from the memory of the accident itself.

Because the memory arrives so unbidden and so completely, Rodrigo has organized much of his waking life around preventing its approach. He has stopped thinking about the event deliberately, cutting the recollection short whenever it begins to surface, pushing it away before it can resolve into its full sequence. He has come to believe, with quiet conviction, that if he allows the memory to complete itself he will not be able to function — that something in him will give way. This has meant avoiding anything that might serve as an on-ramp. He has given up the evening runs he once relied on for decompression, telling his wife he is simply tired, because the physical exertion and elevated heart rate feel too close to the panic of the accident. He has declined invitations to the departmental dinners and social events that once marked his weeks, withdrawing from the pleasures that previously sustained him. These avoidances have not quieted the triggers; if anything, the boundaries of safety have continued to contract. The strategies that were meant to keep the memory at bay have instead preserved its potency — each avoided texture, each rerouted corridor to sidestep Marcus, each cancelled evening reinforces the implicit message that the memory is too dangerous to approach, keeping the triggers charged and the intrusions as forceful as ever.

At work, the consequences have become impossible to ignore. Rodrigo has begun declining complex cases that require extended operative time, citing scheduling conflicts his colleagues have quietly stopped believing. His department chief has asked, with careful tact, whether he is well. It was that conversation, more than anything else, that finally brought him here. Surgery has been the architecture of his identity for three decades, and he is frightened — not of the accident any longer, he says, but of what he is becoming in its aftermath. What he hopes for, with some difficulty articulating it, is to be able to stand in the same room as Marcus without leaving his body.
